title: How Millets Went From Humble Grain to Fine Dining Star Across India and Dubai
excerpt: Chef Shivani Sharma's millet-forward brand Gourmestan is part of a broader movement that has transformed ancient Indian grains into gourmet staples, from Michelin-style restaurants to FMCG shelves.
body:
• Chef Shivani Sharma, a Le Cordon Bleu alumna, has built Gourmestan and Maison Gourmestan into millet-forward brands spanning cloud kitchens, cafés, and FMCG products across India and Dubai.
  • India produces 41% of the world's millet output, and the UN's 2023 International Year of Millets helped catalyze a shift from viewing the grain as a subsistence crop to treating it as a gourmet ingredient.
  • Top Indian restaurants including Indian Accent, Masque, and The Bombay Canteen now feature millet-based dishes, from jowar risottos to ragi brownies, on their tasting menus.
  • Millets require significantly less water than rice and wheat, making them a climate-resilient choice as the food industry grapples with sustainability pressures.

The Chef Behind the Millet Mantra

When Shivani Sharma launched her cloud kitchen in 2016, millets were still largely considered a poor man's grain in urban India. Today, her brand Maison Gourmestan sells millet-based confectionery, artisanal breads, and fromagerie products to a celebrity clientele across Mumbai and Dubai—a trajectory that mirrors the grain's own remarkable rebranding.

Sharma, who holds a Master's in Culinary Arts from Le Cordon Bleu London and degrees from the London School of Economics, Yale, and Michigan State University, identified a gap between everyday staples and elevated gastronomic experiences. Her answer was to apply classical French technique to an ingredient most Indian chefs had overlooked.

"What influenced me to start Gourmestan was that there was nobody working with millets, clean eating and gut-friendly food at the time. I was inspired to create artisanal products using base ingredients that are easily available in the country."

— Shivani Sharma, Founder, Gourmestan

Through Gourmestan, she has introduced gluten-free millet pastries, breads, and cheese alternatives, all locally sourced and manufactured. The brand eschews preservatives in favour of what Sharma calls "simple, wholesome and conscious alternatives." Her Dubai expansion, launched under the Maison Gourmestan banner, includes plans for quick-service restaurants, food trucks, and packaged FMCG products.

From Subsistence Crop to Supergrain

Millets virtually disappeared from Indian fields after the Green Revolution of the 1960s, pushed aside by higher-yielding rice and wheat varieties backed by government subsidies. Their comeback has been decades in the making. India currently produces 41% of the world's millet output, according to the Food and Agriculture Organisation, and the government has aggressively promoted both cultivation and consumption.

The turning point came with the United Nations declaring 2023 the International Year of Millets—a campaign India spearheaded. Data from the Centre for Study of Science, Technology and Policy in Bengaluru suggests that a nationwide shift toward millets could save India 50 million metric tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions and 300 billion cubic metres of water annually, figures that have made the grain attractive to sustainability-conscious restaurants and food brands.

But the real transformation has happened on the plate. Millets such as ragi (finger millet), jowar (sorghum), and bajra (pearl millet) are now being incorporated into contemporary formats: ready-to-eat bowls, artisanal noodles, cookies, craft beers, and high-fibre snacks. The grain's mild flavour and textural versatility—it can be boiled, steamed, toasted, or fermented—have made it a favourite among chefs experimenting with fusion cuisines.

Fine Dining Takes Notice

The shift is visible at India's most celebrated restaurants. At Indian Accent in Delhi, chef Manish Mehrotra has served bajra khichdi with parmesan to international acclaim. Masque in Mumbai, under chef Prateek Sadhu, features foxtail millet with saffron as part of its tasting menu. The Bombay Canteen showcases jowar in three forms—green, boiled, and puffed—in a single salad.

"Millets can be incorporated into a variety of meals as a basic ingredient, a primary element, or a creative garnish. This gives fine-dining food a distinctive and nutritious twist."

— Chef Ankur Sharma, Raahi Neo Bar and Kitchen, Bengaluru

Chefs across the country are turning ragi flour into dimsums and Goan sanna, using millet in risottos with truffles, and crafting saffron-infused millet pilafs. Even desserts have been reimagined: ragi brownies, millet blondies, and foxtail millet crème brûlée now appear on menus from Bengaluru to Chennai. Park Hyatt Chennai's chef Balaji created an entire millet tasting menu featuring sorghum risotto and pearl millet biryani with black chickpeas.

Industry forecasters expect this trajectory to intensify. A report by Entrepreneur India identified millets as a defining ingredient of 2026 dining, noting that "millets will be treated with the reverence once reserved for truffles" as the restaurant industry pivots from imported luxury to indigenous excellence.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For Indians abroad, the millet revival offers a reconnection with ancestral foodways—many diaspora families grew up eating ragi mudde, bajra roti, or jowar bhakri at home, grains their grandparents farmed. The new fine-dining treatment has made these ingredients fashionable in global food circles, making it easier to find millet-based products in cities like Dubai, London, and Singapore.

Sharma's expansion to Dubai is part of this trend. "These regions are highly influenced by brands from Europe, the UK and the US—people here travel very frequently," she told Trend Insider. "There is excellent recall and recognition for brands they have experienced overseas." She plans to expand further into the UK and United States.

What's Next

The millet movement shows no signs of slowing. Dedicated millet restaurants like Millets of Mewar in Udaipur are drawing tourists and health-conscious diners. Breweries have begun releasing millet-based ales. And the Indian government is reportedly considering promoting millet consumption among the armed forces.

For Sharma and her contemporaries, the goal is to make millets not just a menu trend but a pantry staple—bridging the gap between the grain's humble origins and its gourmet future. Whether through a ₹3,000 tasting menu at a five-star hotel or a gluten-free millet cookie delivered to your door in Dubai, the ancient supergrain is staging a comeback that appears built to last.
